question:
A discharge tube containing low-pressure hydrogen gas produces a line spectrum. Consider two different observations:

1) Absorption spectrum of hydrogen gas at room temperature when a continuous spectrum is passed through it.

2) Emission spectrum from excited hydrogen atoms in the discharge tube.

You are given the following statements for this question:

(i) In absorption, a photon can be absorbed only if its energy equals the energy difference between an initial lower energy level and a higher energy level, i.e., $E_\gamma=E_{n_f}-E_{n_i}$ with $n_f>n_i$.

(ii) In emission, a photon is emitted when an atom makes a transition from a higher level to a lower level, i.e., $E_\gamma=E_{n_i}-E_{n_f}$ with $n_i>n_f$.

(iii) At room temperature, the population of hydrogen atoms is overwhelmingly in the ground state $n=1$.

Evaluate why the absorption spectrum of hydrogen gas at room temperature consists almost exclusively of lines belonging to the Lyman series, whereas the emission spectrum contains lines from Balmer, Paschen, etc.

(i) Explain, using the given population statement, why absorption lines must predominantly originate from $n=1$ and hence belong to the Lyman series (core explanation).

(ii) Explain why emission can occur to multiple lower levels ($n_f=1,2,3,\dots$) once atoms are excited, leading to multiple series such as Balmer and Paschen (core explanation).

(iii) Using the energy-level diagram logic, infer why Balmer-series absorption lines are negligible at room temperature without an external preparation of atoms in $n=2$.

options.A: At room temperature, hydrogen atoms are ionized.
options.B: The atmosphere absorbs all visible light, leaving only UV (Lyman) to be detected.
options.C: At room temperature, nearly all atoms are in the ground state ($n=1$), so absorption transitions must start from $n=1$.
options.D: Absorption requires higher energy photons than emission.
